Check whether later experiments in Smit et al. change which protocol does best on CIAR.
Check whether the GPT-3.5-turbo versions match.
Check which of Smit et al.'s debating protocols, if any, corresponds to Liang et al.'s MAD.

in.other_title: No protocol dominates all datasets; debate does not win on reasoning datasets
in.rationale: Liang et al. report that on Counter-Intuitive AR (Table 3), Self-Reflect only marginally improves over the GPT-3.5-Turbo baseline, CoT and Self-Consistency bring more improvements, and their MAD framework, though not as good as GPT-4, outperforms all the other compared methods based on GPT-3.5-Turbo. Smit et al. list CIAR among their reasoning datasets (CosmosQA, CIAR and GPQA, alongside three standard medical datasets) and report that no protocol dominates on all datasets, that Medprompt seems to perform best overall, and that the debating protocols do not outperform the other protocols on the reasoning datasets. Smit et al.'s statement covers the reasoning datasets together rather than CIAR alone, and the compared methods differ (Smit et al. name Medprompt and Ensemble Refinement, Liang et al. name CoT, Self-Consistency and Self-Reflect), so the cited lines do not show a direct contradiction on CIAR. Both papers ask whether debate outperforms other prompting methods, in these different settings.
in.scope: proposed SAME_QUESTION_DIFFERENT_SETTING: whether multi-agent debate outperforms other prompting methods, asked by Liang et al. for counter-intuitive arithmetic reasoning (CIAR) alone, comparing MAD with CoT, Self-Consistency and Self-Reflect based on GPT-3.5-Turbo, and by Smit et al. for the reasoning datasets CosmosQA, CIAR and GPQA together, comparing the debating protocols with other protocols such as Medprompt and Ensemble Refinement
